title: Long-Term Drug Screening Identifies PARP Inhibitors as Irinotecan Combination Partners in BRCA1/2-Wild-Type Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Irinotecan is a component of standard first-line regimens for advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), yet cells that survive irinotecan treatment may retain the capacity to re-establish growth. Most anticancer drug screens use short-term growth inhibition as an initial criterion for compound selection, potentially excluding compounds with limited acute activity. We asked whether some of these excluded candidates might nevertheless show substantial long-term activity and enhance irinotecan responses in combination. Methods: We first screened 3524 compounds for short-term growth inhibition and advanced compounds with limited acute activity to a 10-day colony-growth screen. Long-term hits were narrowed to clinically relevant anticancer agents and then screened with irinotecan. Talazoparib showed the lowest combination-to-single-agent score and was selected for further evaluation. The combination was evaluated across multiple BRCA1/2-wild-type PDAC cell lines and further validated using additional PARP inhibitors and a xenograft model. RNA sequencing and γH2AX analysis were used to examine associated DNA damage-response features. Results: Of the 1877 compounds advanced from the initial 3-day screen, 334 (17.8%) met the long-term hit criterion. In short- versus long-term comparisons, irinotecan plus talazoparib produced greater growth suppression and higher Bliss synergy scores in 10-day than in 72 h assays. Enhanced long-term responses were observed across five BRCA1/2-wild-type PDAC cell lines, and similar long-term effects were observed with three additional PARP inhibitors. The combination also showed synergistic antitumor activity in an MIA PaCa-2 subcutaneous xenograft model. Transcriptomic and γH2AX analyses provided findings consistent with replication-stress and DNA-damage-response processes. Conclusions: A substantial subset of compounds with limited acute activity showed substantial long-term activity. PARP inhibition enhanced irinotecan responses and emerged as a candidate combination strategy in BRCA1/2-wild-type PDAC.

title: The Application Potential and Future Challenges of Plant-Derived Exosome-like Nanoparticles in the Treatment of Liver Diseases.
abstract: Liver disease is a serious global health challenge, with high morbidity and mortality that put significant socioeconomic stress on society. Despite therapeutic advances, current regimens have been limited by rapid drug resistance and insufficient targeting accuracy, and there is an urgent need for new methods. Plant-derived exosome-like nanoparticles (PELNs) are a promising natural nanotherapeutic platform due to their low immunogenicity, high biocompatibility, and prolonged stability in biological fluids. We review the biological sources, basic properties, and key preparative techniques for PELNs and characterize their mechanisms of action and therapeutic use in common liver diseases. We analyze their multiple-target hepatoprotective mechanisms including liver-specific targeting pathways and reducing critical inflammatory and antioxidant cascades. We summarize the therapeutic performance of different PELNs in major hepatic models including hepatocellular carcinoma, hepatic fibrosis, alcohol-related liver disease, and acute liver failure, highlighting key plant sources, primary biological effects, and precise molecular pathways. Moreover, one of the major methodological contributions of this work is the proposal of a new recommended extraction framework based on differential and density gradient centrifugation, optimized specifically for different plant tissue types (leaves, roots/stems, and fruits) to minimize technical heterogeneity. Finally, we discuss the major challenges that impede clinical translation of these nanovesicles, including incompletely elucidated mechanisms, imperfect manufacturing practices, and inadequate safety evaluation mechanisms, pointing to important, useful directions for future applications in hepatology.

title: Bremachlorin-Based Photodynamic-Therapy-Induced Effects in Low-Oxygenated Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC) Tumor Microenvironment.
abstract: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is a minimally invasive treatment whose efficacy is strongly influenced by tumor oxygenation and the tumor microenvironment (TME). Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by severe hypoxia, dense stroma, and immune suppression, limiting therapeutic responsiveness. In this study, we investigated how Bremachlorin-based PDT remodels the TME in two murine PDAC models with distinct immune phenotypes (T-cell-high and T-cell-low) and compared them with the immunogenic MC38 colon carcinoma model. Single-fiber reflectance and fluorescence spectroscopy were used to monitor tumor physiology and photosensitizer dynamics during PDT, while multiplex immunohistochemistry enabled spatial profiling of stromal and immune components post-treatment. PDAC tumors exhibited significantly lower baseline oxygenation than MC38 tumors, which was not substantially improved by reducing the PDT fluence rate from 116 to 50 mW·cm-2. Nevertheless, PDT reduced collagen type I content in both PDAC models, indicating stromal remodeling. Importantly, illumination with a moderate fluence rate of 50 mW·cm-2 significantly increased CD8+ T-cell infiltration and improved the CD8+/neutrophil ratio in T-cell-high PDAC tumors, suggesting a shift toward a less immunosuppressive immune landscape. These findings demonstrate that Bremachlorin-PDT can modulate the PDAC tumor microenvironment and highlight the importance of immune context in shaping PDT outcomes, supporting rational optimization of PDT-based combination therapies.
authors: Thierry P P van den Bosch

title: USP30 Beyond Mitophagy: A Context-Dependent Deubiquitinase in Cancer Progression.
abstract: Ubiquitin-specific protease 30 (USP30) is a mitochondrial outer membrane-associated deubiquitinase best known for antagonizing PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1)/Parkin-dependent ubiquitination and suppressing mitophagy. This established role has linked USP30 to mitochondrial quality control and neurodegenerative diseases. However, emerging studies in cancer have expanded the biological scope of USP30, revealing functions that cannot be explained by mitophagy regulation alone. USP30 regulates diverse cancer-associated substrates through deubiquitination, thereby affecting protein abundance, subcellular localization, protein interactions, and downstream transcriptional programs. These substrate-dependent effects influence mitochondrial dynamics, lipid synthesis, glucose and amino acid metabolism, redox homeostasis, apoptosis, ferroptosis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, cancer stemness, T-cell exhaustion, and therapy resistance. Although most studies indicate tumor-promoting roles of USP30 in hepatocellular carcinoma, breast cancer, colorectal cancer, oral squamous cell carcinoma, ovarian cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, and leukemia models, context-dependent tumor-restraining activities have also been reported. In this Review, we examine cancer-associated functions of USP30 that extend beyond its established role in PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy, discuss the spatial and substrate-dependent mechanisms underlying these activities, and highlight opportunities and challenges for therapeutic targeting.

title: CGRP-RAMP1/CALCRL Signaling Drives TGF-β2-Mediated Immune Evasion and Pancreatic Cancer Progression.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by extensive neural remodeling and a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, both of which contribute to disease progression and therapeutic resistance. However, whether nociceptor-derived signals directly reprogram PDAC cells to promote immune evasion remains poorly understood. Here, we identify a previously unrecognized tumor-intrinsic neuroimmune mechanism driven by calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) signaling through the receptor complex RAMP1/CALCRL on PDAC cells. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of Ramp1 or Calcrl did not alter PDAC cell proliferation in vitro but markedly suppressed tumor growth and prolonged survival in immunocompetent mice. These antitumor effects were lost in immunodeficient hosts, indicating that the pro-tumorigenic function of CGRP signaling depends on an intact host immune system. Consistently, tumor cell-specific loss of Ramp1 or Calcrl remodeled the tumor immune microenvironment, enhancing CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell effector activity. Mechanistically, CGRP stimulation promoted TGF-β2 expression and secretion by PDAC cells in a RAMP1-dependent manner. Tumor-derived TGF-β2 subsequently acted in a paracrine fashion to suppress CD8+ T-cell activation and cytotoxic function, whereas genetic disruption of RAMP1 or pharmacological inhibition of TGF-β signaling relieved this immunosuppression. Together, these findings define a CGRP-RAMP1/CALCRL-TGF-β2 signaling axis through which nociceptive input is converted into tumor-driven adaptive immune evasion in PDAC. This pathway reveals a previously underappreciated mechanism linking neural signaling to PDAC progression and identifies CGRP receptor signaling as a potential therapeutic vulnerability for restoring antitumor immunity and improving the responsiveness of PDAC to immunotherapy.

title: Pretreatment Serum GDF-15 and Features of Clinical Vulnerability in Advanced Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Background: This study aimed to define the clinical significance of pretreatment serum growth differentiation factor-15 (GDF-15), including its associations with clinical vulnerability, survival, and chemotherapy outcomes in advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Methods: Pretreatment serum samples were prospectively collected from 80 patients with locally advanced or metastatic PDAC. GDF-15 was measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and analyzed continuously and according to the cohort median. Associations with clinicopathological characteristics and overall survival (OS) were evaluated in the overall cohort. Treatment effectiveness, delivery, and safety were additionally assessed among 68 patients who received systemic chemotherapy. Results: The median GDF-15 concentration was 362.6 pg/mL. Higher GDF-15 was associated with poor performance status, involvement of multiple metastatic organ sites, an elevated neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, and hypoalbuminemia. Eleven of the 12 patients unable to receive chemotherapy because of clinical deterioration had high GDF-15. The high GDF-15 group had shorter OS than the low GDF-15 group in the overall cohort (median, 6.1 vs. 13.9 months; hazard ratio [HR] = 1.96; 95% CI, 1.23-3.13; p = 0.002). The association between continuous GDF-15 and OS was attenuated and no longer statistically significant after multivariable adjustment (HR per doubling = 1.22; 95% CI, 0.97-1.52; p = 0.085). Among treated patients, progression-free survival and objective response did not differ significantly between groups, whereas high GDF-15 was associated with shorter OS (median, 8.7 vs. 14.2 months; HR = 1.72; 95% CI, 1.02-2.90; p = 0.025) and treatment duration (median, 3.2 vs. 6.3 months; p = 0.007). Relative dose intensity and subsequent treatment rates were similar. Febrile neutropenia occurred exclusively in the high GDF-15 group, which also accounted for four of five treatment-related deaths. Conclusions: Elevated pretreatment GDF-15 was associated with limited treatment fitness and inferior survival in patients with advanced PDAC, without clear evidence of intrinsic chemotherapy resistance. GDF-15 may represent a potential marker of systemic vulnerability in advanced PDAC, although its clinical utility requires external validation.

title: Integrated Bile Metabolomics and Serum Biomarkers for Differentiating Cholangiocarcinoma from Cholelithiasis.
abstract: Background: We investigated bile metabolites and serum variables for differentiating cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) from cholelithiasis. Methods: Bile from 31 patients with CCA and 48 with cholelithiasis was profiled by high-resolution LC-MS. Candidate metabolites and serum variables were integrated in a seven-variable classifier, and public single-cell data provided tissue-level biological context. Results: Of 2269 annotated metabolite features, 532 met the exploratory screening criteria. The selected signature comprised pyruvic acid, lipoxin A4, CEA, APOA1, 3-chloro-L-tyrosine, ADP-ribose, and glutaric acid; pyruvic acid had the largest contribution in the SHAP analysis. Random forest achieved an AUC of 0.894 in the classifier comparison, a training cross-validation AUC of 0.820, and an AUC of 0.914 in the 16-patient test subset. Because selection used all 79 patients before evaluation, these internal performance estimates may be optimistic. Conclusions: Integrated bile and serum profiling identified a promising seven-variable signature for differentiating CCA from cholelithiasis in this cohort. Added diagnostic value over routine serum markers and performance in other benign biliary conditions have not been established.

title: Culture Dimensionality Shapes Drug Sensitivity to Kinase Inhibitor Combinations with Epigenetic or Metabolic Inhibition in a Hepatocellular Carcinoma Model.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains one of the deadliest malignancies worldwide, and treatment efficacy is often limited by tumor heterogeneity and therapy resistance. Preclinical models, particularly three-dimensional (3D) cell cultures, are increasingly used to better mimic the tumor microenvironment and improve the predictive value of drug testing. This study aimed to compare the effectiveness of different pharmacological treatments for HCC in two-dimensional (2D) monolayer and 3D spheroid HepG2 culture models and to investigate the underlying cell death mechanisms. The multikinase inhibitors sorafenib and regorafenib, the epigenetic histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor panobinostat, and the metabolic phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH) inhibitor NCT-503 were evaluated as single agents and in combination. Results: All tested compounds induced cell death and reduced cellular ATP levels in both 2D and 3D systems. Combination treatments of sorafenib or regorafenib with either panobinostat or NCT-503 generally showed no significant deviation from additivity in cytotoxicity and cellular energy levels, although significant sub-additive deviations were observed for some panobinostat combinations in the ATP analyses. Mechanistically, panobinostat induced apoptotic cell death, as indicated by caspase-3 and PARP cleavage, increased caspase-3/7 activity, and inhibition by the pan-caspase inhibitor zVAD-FMK, whereas NCT-503-mediated cell death occurred largely independently of canonical caspase-mediated apoptosis in 2D cultures. Although similar effects were observed in 3D spheroids, cell death responses were attenuated compared with 2D cultures, whereas reductions in cellular ATP levels remained comparable, indicating a differentiated relationship between ATP depletion and cell death in 2D and 3D cultures. Conclusions: In summary, combining tyrosine kinase inhibition with epigenetic or metabolic targeting agents increased cell death and impaired cellular energy homeostasis more effectively than single-agent treatment in HepG2 cells, with no significant deviation from additivity detected in most combination analyses. Notably, 3D-cultured HepG2 cells showed attenuated cell death responses despite comparable reductions in cellular ATP levels, highlighting differences in drug responses between 2D and 3D culture models. These findings support the use of 3D culture models as a complementary approach to conventional 2D systems for evaluating drug responses, particularly as they reveal an attenuated cell death response compared with 2D cultures.

title: Current Evidence on Gene-Based and Epigenetic Therapeutic, Diagnostic, and Prognostic Strategies in Epithelial-Derived Carcinomas: A Scoping Review.
abstract: Background: Epithelial-derived carcinomas exhibit genomic instability due to genetic mutation and epigenetic dysregulation. Mechanisms such as DNA methylation, histone modifications, and noncoding RNA regulation may lead to tumor progression, immune evasion, and treatment resistance. Presently, gene-based and epigenetic therapies, including CRISPR systems, RNA interference, and chromatin-modifying agents, are reported to be effective in targeted cancer treatment. Objectives: This scoping review aims to map the evidence on gene-based technologies in epithelial-derived carcinomas, including therapeutic, diagnostic, prognostic, screening, and disease-modeling applications, and to identify molecular targets, translational outcomes, and gaps in the current evidence base. The review will characterize the molecular targets, gene-based approaches, cancer types, translational applications, and reported outcomes to identify evidence gaps, translational challenges, and priorities for future research. Methods: The scoping review was conducted as per PRISMA-ScR by conducting a literature search in databases such as PubMed, Embase, and Google Scholar, covering studies published between 2016 and 2026. In the inclusion criteria, all studies and reviews related to investigating gene-based, RNA-mediated, and epigenetic therapies in epithelial cancers were included. Thirty-six studies met the eligibility criteria. Results: Amongst the studies reviewed, the most common epithelial cancers reported were hepatocellular carcinoma, ovarian carcinoma, lung carcinoma, and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Among the epithelial-derived carcinomas identified in this review, HCC was the most frequently represented cancer; epigenetic alterations and therapies used were RNA-based therapies, CRISPR diagnostics, and epigenetic drugs. Ovarian and breast cancers targeting BRCA pathways and chromatin remodeling produced clinical translation outcomes. Lung and colorectal cancers showed moderate epigenetic involvement, often managed through combined therapeutic strategies. Pancreatic cancer therapies were limited by challenges in drug delivery despite identifiable molecular targets. Gene therapies such as CRISPR-based gene editing, RNAi/siRNA therapies, miRNA/lncRNA targeting, and HDAC inhibition were commonly reported. Conclusions: The present study indicates that the majority of epithelial-derived carcinomas can benefit from gene-based and epigenetic therapies. Though the majority of carcinomas, such as hepatocellular, have good clinical outcomes, pancreatic cancer has limited clinical translation.

title: Mexican Oregano Infusion and Carvacrol Modify Cytokine Concentration, Induce Apoptosis, and Regulate Antioxidant Enzyme Expression and Function in Breast Cancer Cell Lines: Implications for Bioactive Molecule-Based Therapeutics.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Background/Objectives: Breast cancer (BC), particularly aggressive subtypes such as triple-negative TNBC, remains a significant clinical challenge due to treatment resistance and therapeutic toxicity. This study evaluated the antitumor potential, antioxidant activity, and anti-inflammatory effect of Mexican Oregano (Lippia graveolens) infusion (MoI) and its bioactive constituent, carvacrol (Cv), in diverse BC cell lines (MCF-7, HCC-1954, and MDA-MB-231).
METHODS: Cellular responses were assessed by quantifying apoptosis, profiling cytokines (IL-4, IL-6, IL-10), and analyzing the gene expression of antioxidant enzymes (CAT, SOD2, GPX1) and their enzymatic activities.
RESULTS: Cv exhibited potent, subtype-independent pro-apoptotic activity, while MoI demonstrated significant efficacy with attenuated cytotoxicity in non-tumoral HaCaT cells. Both treatments mediated complex modification of cytokine signaling, characterized by reduction in the extracellular concentration of tumor-promoting IL-4, IL-6, and IL-10, an effect most pronounced in the highly aggressive MDA-MB-231 cell line. Transcriptional and functional analyses further revealed that these agents alter the expression and activity of antioxidant enzymes, thereby promoting pro-oxidant environments conducive to cancer cell death.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings indicate that MoI and Cv exert antitumor effects through coordinated pathways of apoptosis induction, extracellular cytokine levels and redox disruption. Consequently, MoI emerges as a promising candidate for complementary therapeutic strategies in BC management, particularly for aggressive subtypes, owing to its impact on inflammatory networks and redox vulnerabilities. At the same time, Cv serves as a compelling lead compound for targeted oncological research.

title: Longitudinal Circulating Nerve Growth Factor in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: An Exploratory Study of Postoperative Recurrence and First-Line Disease Control.
abstract: Nerve growth factor (NGF) signaling is involved in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) neurotropism, perineural invasion, pain, and tumor-stromal crosstalk, but its value as a circulating biomarker remains poorly defined. We retrospectively analyzed 51 patients with PDAC who underwent serial liquid-biopsy assessment across perioperative and advanced-disease timepoints. Circulating β-NGF was assessed in plasma, and samples without measurable NGF were classified as non-detectable. NGF was analyzed as both a zero-inflated continuous variable and a binary detectable/non-detectable biomarker. Phase-aligned associations with recurrence, disease-free survival, first-line progression-free survival, CA19-9, CEA, TGFβ, PD-L1, pain, and pathological perineural invasion were evaluated using non-parametric and permutation-based methods with false-discovery-rate adjustment. NGF availability was highest at first-line treatment initiation, where 9 of 40 patients had detectable NGF (22.5%). The clearest signal emerged postoperatively: patients who subsequently recurred had higher NGF values than those who did not (median 25.5 pg/mL vs. non-detectable; nominal p = 0.038). Detectable postoperative NGF was directionally associated with recurrence, while detectable NGF at first-line treatment initiation was associated with numerically shorter progression-free survival. Pooled active-disease measurements did not show a clear NGF increase versus postoperative samples, arguing against a generic disease-burden signal. No association remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction; therefore, all observed signals should be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating. These findings support prospective validation of circulating NGF within multimarker liquid-biopsy strategies focused on postoperative recurrence, perineural invasion-related biology, and treatment resistance in PDAC.

title: SFPQ Promotes Hepatocellular Carcinoma Progression by Affecting GTF2H3 Splicing Variants.
abstract: Background: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), the predominant type of liver cancer, exhibits a high mortality rate due to unclear molecular mechanisms and limited biomarkers. Accumulating evidence indicates that splicing factors (SFs) can promote tumor cell proliferation, invasion, metastasis, and drug resistance by altering the splicing patterns of target genes. However, the regulatory mechanisms underlying SF-mediated alternative splicing (AS) are highly intricate, and the specific functions and pathways of SFs in HCC initiation and progression remain to be further elucidated. Methods: First, Cox regression and LASSO regression analyses of splicing factors (SFs) were performed using the TCGA database, followed by validation using the ICGC dataset. The prognostic value of SFPQ was assessed with the Kaplan-Meier plotter. Next, the potential association of SFPQ with the immune microenvironment of HCC was explored using TIMER and CIBERSORT. In addition, we screened AS events associated with SFPQ expression in TCGA-LIHC, conducted GO/KEGG pathway enrichment analyses, and investigated the correlation between GTF2H3 percent spliced in index (PSI) values and clinicopathological features in HCC patients. Finally, the effect of targeting the exon 10- or exon 11-containing variants of GTF2H3 on HCC was examined at the cellular level. Results: LASSO regression analysis identified five key SFs significantly associated with HCC prognosis, including SFPQ, HTRA2, DAZAP1, PCBP2, and YBX1. Among these, SFPQ was determined as the most critical SF influencing HCC survival, and its overexpression was positively correlated with HCC progression. GO and KEGG analyses revealed that the pathways potentially associated with SFPQ include metabolic pathways, oxidative phosphorylation, mRNA surveillance pathway, and the PPAR signaling pathway. Furthermore, SFPQ expression was associated with the exclusion of exons 10 and 11 of the GTF2H3 gene. Computational analysis also suggested a potential link between SFPQ and immune cell infiltration. Targeting the exon 11-containing variant of GTF2H3 significantly reduced cell viability and migration of HCC cells. Conclusion: SFPQ expression is elevated in HCC and correlates with tumor aggressiveness and poor patient prognosis. Our findings suggest that SFPQ may influence HCC progression through its association with the GTF2H3 exon 10/11 ME event and the immune microenvironment. However, further experimental validation is required to confirm these mechanisms. Our findings suggest that SFPQ may serve as a promising biomarker and therapeutic candidate for HCC.

title: Tumor-educated macrophages promote ferroptosis inhibition in pancreatic cancer via activating the p62-KEAP1-NRF2 pathway.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic cancer is one of the most aggressive and lethal gastrointestinal malignancies, and ferroptosis resistance contributes to chemoresistance. Tumor-educated macrophages(TAMs) are key components of the tumor microenvironment, but whether and how they regulate ferroptosis in pancreatic cancer cells remains largely unknown. This study aimed to investigate the regulatory role of tumor-educated macrophages (TEMs) in pancreatic cancer cell ferroptosis and the underlying molecular mechanism.
METHODS: TEMs were generated by coculturing THP-1 cells with the pancreatic cancer cell lines PANC1 and CFPAC, and TEM-conditioned medium (TEM-CM) was collected to treat pancreatic cancer cells. Ferroptosis was induced by erastin, and ferroptotic events were assessed by lipid ROS, MDA, iron accumulation, GSH levels, and transmission electron microscopy. RNA sequencing was performed to identify differentially expressed genes. The expression and activity of VEGFR2, C-Raf, ERK1/2, mTOR, LC3, p62, KEAP1, and NRF2 were investigated by treating cells with pharmacological inhibitors (Ki8751, LY3009120, chloroquine, and ferrostatin-1), performing gene knockdown and overexpression, and conducting Western blot co-immunoprecipitation, ubiquitination, and cycloheximide chase assays. In vivo experiments were conducted using an orthotopic mouse model of pancreatic cancer (n = 5 per group).
RESULTS: TEM-CM reduced the sensitivity of PANC1 and CFPAC cells to erastin-induced ferroptosis, as evidenced by decreased lipid ROS, MDA, and iron accumulation and increased GSH levels. Neutralization of VEGF, but not IL-10 or TGFβ, significantly reversed the ferroptosis-inhibiting effect of TEM-CM. RNA sequencing identified TM7SF2 as a key mediator. TEM-CM upregulated TM7SF2 mRNA and protein levels, activated mTOR, and suppressed autophagy, leading to p62 accumulation. Accumulated p62 competitively bound KEAP1, disrupted the KEAP1-NRF2 interaction, inhibited NRF2 ubiquitination and degradation, and promoted NRF2 nuclear translocation, thereby upregulating GPX4, HMOX1, and GCLM. Mechanistically, TEM-derived VEGF bound VEGFR2 and activated the C-Raf/ERK1/2 pathway by upregulating TM7SF2, which in turn promoted mTOR phosphorylation. These effects were reversed by TM7SF2 knockdown, VEGF neutralization, VEGFR2 inhibition, or C-Raf inhibition.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that TEM-derived VEGF promotes ferroptosis resistance in pancreatic cancer cells through the VEGFR2-TM7SF2-C-Raf/ERK1/2-mTOR-autophagy-p62-NRF2 axis. This axis may represent a potential therapeutic target for overcoming ferroptosis resistance in pancreatic cancer. However, our conclusions are mainly based on in vitro cell models, and further validation in additional cell lines, patient-derived organoids, and in vivo models is warranted.

title: Metabolic sensing in 3D models of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: probing pH, oxygen, and lactate dynamics to decode chemoresistance.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the deadliest malignancies due to its late diagnosis, extensive desmoplasia, and strong chemoresistance. Recent advances in three-dimensional (3D) in vitro modelling have provided new insights into tumor-stroma interactions and metabolic adaptations that drive disease progression. This review summarizes the pathogenesis and tumor microenvironment (TME) hallmarks of PDAC, emphasizing the metabolic heterogeneity characterized by altered pH, oxygen, and lactate gradients. It discusses conventional and emerging therapeutic strategies, the molecular basis of drug resistance, and the role of the TME in treatment failure. Furthermore, it highlights the evolution of 3D experimental models as physiologically relevant tools to study PDAC biology and evaluate drug efficacy. Special attention is given to the integration of optical biosensors for non-invasive spatio-temporal monitoring of pH and metabolic fluctuations. These sensing technologies, coupled with advanced bioengineered models, are paving the way for precision oncology and patient-tailored strategies in pancreatic cancer.

title: USP22-mediated phagocytic evasion promotes immune escape in TP53-inactivated hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/AIMS: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Here, we aimed to elucidate the tumor cell-intrinsic functions of ubiquitin-specific protease 22 (USP22) in the immune escape of HCC cells.
METHODS: Autochthonous mouse models of HCC with either genetic Usp22 loss or Trp53 knockdown were used. In vitro and in vivo phagocytosis assays were performed to evaluate the interactions between HCC cells and macrophages. Multicolor fluorescence, spatial transcriptomics, immunoprecipitation and ubiquitination assays were used to explore the potential underlying mechanisms.
RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS: We observed that tumor cell-intrinsic USP22 inhibits the infiltration and anticancer function of tumoricidal macrophages in HCC. USP22 expression in HCC cells blocks their direct phagocytosis by tumoricidal macrophages. Mechanistically, CD24 (a known phagocytosis checkpoint) mediates USP22-induced suppression of phagocytosis. USP22 promotes the transcriptional expression of CD24 by deubiquitinating and stabilizing the transcription factor E2F7. Furthermore, wild-type p53 downregulates USP22 protein expression, whereas TP53 inactivation markedly upregulates USP22 protein expression. The USP22-E2F7-CD24 axis is responsible for mediating TP53-inactivation-induced phagocytic evasion and hepatocarcinogenesis. Mechanistically, USP22 proteins bind to one another and suppress ubiquitination at the K442 residue. The wild-type p53 protein disrupts this mutual deubiquitination, thereby facilitating USP22 degradation. Moreover, TNF secreted by tumoricidal macrophages promotes USP22 degradation by disrupting its self-stabilizing mechanism in a wild-type p53-dependent manner. Our findings indicate that USP22-E2F7-CD24 axis-mediated phagocytic evasion promotes immune escape in TP53-inactivated HCC.

title: Exosome-Inspired Proteolipid Nanoparticles Enable Safe, Extrahepatic RNAi-Chemo Therapy Through Cholesterol-Free, Tumor-Preferential Delivery.
abstract: Lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-enabled genetic medicines are reshaping cancer therapy yet remain constrained by liver-biased tropism, dose-limiting toxicities, and limited efficacy in refractory solid tumors such as pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Here, exosome-inspired proteolipid nanoparticles (Em-pLNPs) are developed to embed three exosomal membrane proteins within an ionizable lipid matrix to support safe, extrahepatic delivery of combinatorial gene-chemo payloads. Em-pLNPs are generated by one-step microfluidic mixing to incorporate the tetraspanins CD63 and CD81 and the "don't-eat-me" marker CD47 into the lipid shell, co-encapsulate diverse nucleic acid and small-molecule cargos, and enable modular CD44-targeted surface functionalization. Following systemic administration in orthotopic PDAC models, Em-pLNPs exhibit prolonged circulation, preferential extrahepatic tumor accumulation, deep penetration of desmoplastic stroma, and efficient cytosolic delivery, while markedly improving tissue tolerability relative to ligand-decorated clinical LNP benchmarks. Formulated with an RNAi-chemo cocktail (siKRAS, siIL-6, and gemcitabine), Em-pLNPs permit repeated intravenous dosing that drives robust, synergistic tumor regression and mitigates chemoresistance. By coupling exosome-like immune evasion and tissue tropism with the manufacturability and high gene-loading capacity of LNPs, Em-pLNPs define a translational proteolipid platform for safe extrahepatic gene therapy against refractory solid tumors.

title: A Synergetic Hybrid Multienzyme: Remodeling Tumor Microenvironment to Simultaneously Activate NK Cells and T Cells for Enhanced Catalytic Immunotherapy of Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
abstract: Hybrid multienzymes integrating natural enzymes and nanozymes are promising for reactive oxygen species (ROS)-mediated tumor catalytic immunotherapy. However, traditional hybrid multienzymes exhibit weak catalytic synergy with insufficient ROS production. These limitations are particularly pronounced in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) featuring sophisticated antioxidant systems and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, factors that compromise catalytic therapy and induce the dysfunction of NK and T cells. Herein, a synergetic CuSe@GOD hybrid multienzyme is constructed via in situ growth of peroxidase-like CuSe nanozymes within the cavities of glucose oxidase (GOD). The confined intracavity catalytic space boosts CuSe nanozyme catalytic activity and enables strong catalytic synergy with GOD. In HCC cells, GOD-produced H2O2 is rapidly transformed into ROS by confined CuSe nanozymes. Meanwhile, Cu2 + reduction-triggered glutathione depletion and selenium species-mediated thioredoxin reductase inactivation disrupts dual antioxidant systems to amplify ROS levels, while intracellular copper overload induces cuproptosis. Notably, ROS-induced oxidative stress upregulates NKG2DL in HCC cells to restore NK cell function and facilitates mitochondrial DNA release during cuproptosis for cGAS-STING pathway activation and subsequent T cell recruitment. Overall, this study establishes a synergetic hybrid multienzyme to simultaneously activate NK and T cells, offering a promising direction for HCC catalytic immunotherapy.

title: Fibroblast-myeloid stromal crosstalk is associated with clinicopathological diversity in intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms of the pancreas.
abstract: Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN), a grossly visible precursor of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, is classified into gastric, intestinal, and pancreatobiliary subtypes, each associated with distinct clinicopathological features and biological aggressiveness. We hypothesised that the tumour microenvironment can explain the association between histological subtypes and clinical outcomes. We first enrolled 116 IPMN resection cases, with or without associated invasive carcinoma, and then sequenced four single-nucleus RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) libraries from those with distinct histological grades and subtypes. The snRNA-seq revealed that fibroblasts were the main source of cell-cell communication, whereas myeloid and mast cells were the main receivers. Therefore, we subclassified fibroblasts into inflammatory (iCAF), myofibroblast (myCAF), and reticular-like (rCAF) subpopulations, and myeloid cells into monocytes, neutrophils, macrophages, and dendritic cell subpopulations. Cell-cell interaction analysis revealed that iCAF and rCAF mainly communicated with SPP1High macrophages via the C3-integrin pathway and with neutrophils via the CXCL12-CXCR4 pathway, whereas myCAF mainly communicated with monocytes and mast cells via ECM-related pathways. Subsequently, we performed two panels of Opal multiplex immunohistochemistry and Elastic van Gieson staining to evaluate fibroblast and myeloid subpopulations and collagen, respectively, in all enrolled cases. Quantitative image analyses revealed that iCAF, neutrophils, and SPP1+ macrophages were associated with higher histological grade, whereas myCAF, collagen, monocytes, and mast cells were associated with lower histological grade. No decrease in myCAF or increase in neutrophils was observed in the invasive intestinal type. Finally, we classified the cases into three groups based on the density of fibroblast and myeloid subpopulations: iCAF/SPP1+ macrophage-rich (I-stroma), neutrophil-rich (N-stroma), and myCAF/mast cell-rich (M-stroma). These stromal groups were associated with distinct clinicopathological features. In conclusion, we revealed that the heterogeneous microenvironment of IPMN, associated with distinct clinicopathological features, may explain the clinical significance of histological subtypes.

title: Coupling oxidative de-stabilization with immune activation overcomes radioresistance in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Radioresistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a coordinated adaptive state rather than failure of a single pathway, sustained by reinforced redox buffering and suppressed immune activation. Strategies that intensify radiation damage without disrupting this state have shown limited efficacy. We sought to determine whether radiosensitization can be achieved by destabilizing tumor oxidative homeostasis while restoring immune competence.
METHODS: A BSA-templated Fe/Mn nanoassembly incorporating the thiol-reactive agent RRX-001 and folate targeting (BFMR-FA) was developed as a multifunctional and MRI-visible platform. Its biological effects were evaluated across radioresistant cellular systems, organoids, and orthotopic tumor models.
RESULTS: BFMR-FA shifts the redox equilibrium of tumor cells beyond a recoverable threshold. By depleting glutathione and suppressing the SLC7A11-GPX4 axis, it converts radiation-induced oxidative stress from a transient signal into sustained lipid peroxidation, resulting in convergent ferroptotic and apoptotic cell death. This transition is accompanied by the emergence of immunogenic stress signals and activation of the STING-TBK1-IRF3 pathway, enabling dendritic cell maturation and expansion of cytotoxic T-cell responses. In vivo, these effects translate into near-complete suppression of radioresistant tumor growth with systemic tolerance. The Fe/Mn composition enables direct visualization of intratumoral delivery by T1-weighted MRI.
CONCLUSION: These findings support a model in which radiosensitization is achieved not by amplifying tumor damage alone, but by collapsing the adaptive redox state that constrains it. The resulting oxidative destabilization coupled with immune activation defines an oxidative homeostasis collapse-driven radio-immuno synergy, providing a generalizable framework for overcoming therapeutic resistance in solid tumors.

title: Comparative characterization of OncoPro™ and Wnt-based media reveals distinct phenotypic and pharmacologic states in patient-derived tumor organoids.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patient-derived tumor organoids (PDTOs) are strongly influenced by culture medium. We compared OncoPro™ (OP) Tumoroid Culture medium with conventional Wnt/R-spondin/noggin (Wnt) medium. This recently developed OP medium offers a standardized, serum-free alternative to Wnt-based formulations.
METHODS: We compared OP and Wnt media across 36 PDTO lines from various malignancies (colorectal, pancreatic, breast, lung, gastric, gastroesophageal junction, biliary head and neck and unknown primary), assessing establishment success. Selected PDTO models were subjected to downstream characterization, including morphological assessment and bulk transcriptomic profiling with comparison to public single-cell RNA sequencing reference datasets (n = 11), whole-exome sequencing (WES) (n = 9), and pharmacological response profiling to a 33-drug panel (n = 3).
RESULTS: Adaptation from Wnt medium to OP succeeded in 83.3% (15/18), whereas de novo establishment favored Wnt (33.3% vs 11.1%). Key oncogenic driver alterations were retained across matched organoid cultures, supporting preservation of tumor-relevant genomic features. Transcriptomic profiling confirmed preserved tumor-identity across media, while revealing different epithelial state programs: Wnt upregulated proliferation/stemness-associated genes (e.g. LGR5) and OP enriched adhesion-associated genes and inflammatory/TGF-β programs. In scRNA databases OP signatures preferentially mapped to malignant epithelial compartments in pancreatic cancer, whereas Wnt signatures were linked to non-malignant epithelium. Similarly, in colon cancer OP signature mapped predominantly to the malignant epithelial compartments. Drug (n = 33) screening in pancreatic- and colorectal cancer PDTOs (n = 3) demonstrated consistent medium-dependent shifts: Wnt-grown PDTOs were globally more sensitive in the screened subset, particularly to MAPK-axis inhibitors and apoptosis-sensitizers, while OP-grown PDTOs exhibited relative resistance.
CONCLUSIONS: Culture medium composition is a key determinant of PDTO phenotype, transcriptome and drug sensitivity. Wnt medium was associated with drug-sensitive states, whereas OP medium was associated with adhesion- and inflammatory-related programs, relative resistance in the screened subset of 33 drugs and closer alignment with malignant epithelial programs in the analyzed pancreatic / colorectal cancer single-cell atlases.

title: Stromal CCL2/CXCL10/SPARC axes drive pro-tumor CHI3L1 expression for microenvironmental modulation in pancreatic cancer progression and therapeutic innovation.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chitinase-3-like-protein 1 (CHI3L1), a low-abundance protein in normal tissues, is markedly upregulated in the pancreatic tumor microenvironment (TME), where it promotes fibrosis and immune evasion. Spatial transcriptomics revealed enrichment of CHI3L1 at tumor-stroma interfaces, suggesting that cell-cell interactions regulate CHI3L1 expression.
METHODS: We employed 2D and 3D multicellular culture models, incorporating pancreatic cancer cells, macrophages, and pancreatic stellate cells (PSCs), to recapitulate TME-mediated CHI3L1 induction. Mechanistic insights were gained through secretome profiling, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP), and methylation-specific PCR. The therapeutic potential of targeting identified axes was evaluated in an orthotopic pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC) mouse model.
RESULTS: We identified CCL2, CXCL10, and SPARC as key secreted mediators during tumor-stroma crosstalk that cooperatively induced CHI3L1 expression in cancer cells via activation of NF-κB and STAT3. Specifically, inflammatory cytokines within the TME recruited macrophages to induce CCL2, which, in concert with PSCs, enhances CXCL10 and SPARC secretion. Mechanistically, NF-κB directly bound the CHI3L1 promoter, while STAT3 reduced DNA methyltransferase 1 levels, leading to promoter hypomethylation and epigenetic activation of CHI3L1. Clinically, high CHI3L1 expression correlated with the upregulated stromal CCL2, CXCL10, and SPARC levels, and the combined four-marker signature was an independent prognostic factor for both overall and disease-free survival in multivariable analysis. In vivo, blockade of the upstream stromal pathways (CCR2/CXCR3/TGFβR1) coupled with CHI3L1 neutralization reduced tumor growth and remodeled the immunosuppressive microenvironment in immunocompetent PDAC models.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings uncover a cooperative multicellular signaling network that orchestrates CHI3L1 expression in cancer via transcriptional and epigenetic reprogramming. Disrupting these upstream stromal pathways concurrently with CHI3L1 neutralization was associated with reduced T-cell exhaustion, offering a promising combinatorial approach for PDAC immunotherapy.

title: Topographic mapping of the HCC microenvironment reveals an antitumor axis between CCL19+ fibroblasts and CXCR3+ B Cells.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a critical role in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression, yet the spatial interactions among its cellular components remain poorly understood. This study aimed to map the spatial gene expression signatures of primary HCC with or without portal vein tumor thrombus (PVTT) and to investigate the spatial crosstalk between cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and B cells, as well as its clinical relevance.
METHODS: Spatial transcriptomic sequencing was performed on primary HCC tissues from patients with or without PVTT to characterize regional heterogeneity and identify potential CAF-B cell interactions. Findings were validated using public single-cell RNA-seq datasets and a subcutaneous H22 hepatoma mouse model. We further established a fully murine CAF-derived CCL19 validation model by co-inoculating Hepa1-6 cells with JS1-Vector or JS1-mCCL19 fibroblasts, with or without anti-mouse CXCR3 blockade. Multiplex immunofluorescence staining and multi-center clinical cohorts were employed to assess the prognostic value of the identified interaction axis.
RESULTS: Stromal and border regions of non-metastatic HCC exhibited heightened immune activity and enrichment of tertiary lymphoid structures. Spatial transcriptomics revealed co-localization of CAFs and B cells, with cell communication analysis identifying the CCL19-CXCR3 axis as a key mediator. In vivo, CAF-derived CCL19 promoted B cell infiltration and suppressed tumor growth in a CXCR3-dependent manner. In the JS1-mCCL19 model, fibroblast-derived CCL19 significantly inhibited tumor growth and increased tumor-infiltrating B cells, whereas CXCR3 blockade partly reversed both effects. Clinically, CCL19⁺ CAFs and CXCR3⁺ B cells infiltration were positively correlated, and their high co-infiltration predicted significantly longer overall survival in HCC patients.
CONCLUSION: This study uncovers a novel spatial immunoregulatory module in which CAFs recruit CXCR3⁺ B cells via CCL19 to restrain HCC progression. These findings provide new insights into TME architecture and offer potential prognostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets for HCC.

title: Integrated multi-omics analysis reveals that tumour cell-intrinsic DCLK1 is associated with an angiogenic tumour microenvironment in cholangiocarcinoma via NF-κB/CXCL5.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) is an aggressive malignancy with a poor prognosis and complex tumour microenvironment. We previously demonstrated that doublecortin-like kinase 1 (DCLK1) is associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in CCA; however, its biological functions and clinical relevance remain unclear. Herein, we elucidated the role of DCLK1 in CCA progression, focusing on its effects on angiogenesis, and evaluated its potential as a prognostic marker.
METHODS: We analysed bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing data to characterise DCLK1 expression and function in CCA. Functional validation was performed using conditioned medium from DCLK1-modified CCA cells, as well as endothelial tube formation, migration, and invasion assays. Tumour vascular density was assessed using a xenograft model. We used a human angiogenesis-related antibody array, western blotting, quantitative real-time PCR, and nuclear translocation assays to examine CXCL5 expression and NF-κB pathway activity.
RESULT: We found that DCLK1 was upregulated in CCA and correlated with advanced disease and poor survival. DCLK1⁺ malignant cells displayed pro-angiogenic features and increased paracrine interaction with endothelial cells. Conditioned medium from DCLK1-overexpressing tumour cells enhanced endothelial tube formation, migration, and invasion, whereas DCLK1 knockout reversed these effects. DCLK1-expressing tumours showed increased vascular density in vivo. Mechanistically, an angiogenesis antibody array and western blotting demonstrated that DCLK1 activated the NF-κB pathway to upregulate CXCL5 expression. Pharmacological inhibition of NF-κB or neutralization of CXCL5 significantly attenuated DCLK1-related pro-angiogenic responses in vitro.
CONCLUSION: DCLK1 activated the NF-κB pathway to upregulate CXCL5 secretion; inhibiting NF-κB or CXCL5 reduced DCLK1-related pro-angiogenic capacity.
journal: Journal of cancer research and clinical oncology

title: Intestinal Candida albicans promotes HCC progression and anti-PD-1 resistance via IL-17A and Trem2+ macrophages.
abstract:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: Whether intestinal fungal dysbiosis contributes to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression and resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) remains unclear. We investigated how gut Candida albicans influences HCC progression, immune remodeling, and response to ICI therapy.
METHODS: Fecal and tumor samples from patients with HCC, liver cirrhosis, and healthy controls were analyzed using ITS2 sequencing, immune profiling, and correlation analyses. Mechanistic studies focused on four complementary autochthonous murine HCC models and cell-based assays, integrating single-cell and bulk RNA sequencing, genetic and pharmacologic perturbations, Kaede photoconversion, fungal antigen recall assays, antifungal treatment, and anti-PD-1 therapy.
RESULTS: Fecal C. albicans abundance was higher in HCC patients and was associated with advanced disease, shorter overall survival, and reduced durable clinical benefit. Across HCC models, C. albicans gavage increased tumor burden and induced a Th17/IL-17A-skewed microenvironment characterized by Trem2+ macrophage accumulation and impaired CD8+ T cell infiltration and function. Antifungal treatment attenuated tumor progression, whereas IL-17A blockade or deficiency largely abrogated C. albicans-associated tumor promotion. Mechanistically, IL-17A induced tumor-derived MCP-1 through ACT1-TRAF6-TAK1 signaling to recruit macrophages and upregulated PAI-1, which activated TGF-β/Smad3 signaling to promote an immunosuppressive Trem2+ macrophage state. These macrophages limited CD8+ T cell recruitment and effector function through coordinated CXCL10 repression and GAL-1 induction, while potentially reinforcing Th17 responses through IL-1β and IL-6. Kaede photoconversion demonstrated enhanced mesenteric lymph node-to-liver Th17 trafficking, while fungal antigen recall assays revealed preferential Th17 responsiveness to C. albicans. C. albicans also impaired anti-PD-1 efficacy in vivo, whereas antifungal treatment partially restored therapeutic responsiveness.
CONCLUSIONS: Intestinal C. albicans promotes HCC progression and anti-PD-1 resistance through an IL-17A-Trem2+ macrophage circuit, supporting its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target.
IMPACT AND IMPLICATIONS: Intestinal fungal dysbiosis is increasingly recognized as a component of the gut-liver axis, but its functional contribution to HCC has remained poorly defined. Our study identifies intestinal Candida albicans as a promoter of HCC progression in experimental models and delineates an IL-17A-MCP-1/PAI-1-Trem2+ macrophage circuit that links fungal exposure to impaired CD8+ T-cell immunity and reduced response to PD-1 blockade. These findings are relevant to researchers and clinicians seeking microbiome-associated determinants of HCC progression and immunotherapy resistance. Fecal C. albicans abundance and components of this immune circuit may warrant evaluation as biomarkers for patient stratification and as potential targets for combination therapy. However, the clinical associations reported here are based on modest observational cohorts, and antifungal treatment was tested as a proof-of-concept intervention in mice. Larger prospective studies and more selective therapeutic approaches will therefore be required before these findings can inform clinical management.

title: Patient-Derived Organoids from cryopreserved tissue can represent clinically relevant tools for drug testing in Biliary Cancer.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Patient-derived organoids (PDO) are three-dimensional cultures established from cancer tissues. While PDOs can replicate morphology and drug sensitivity of cancer from given patients, their clinical applicability is limited by their lack of integration in clinical trials. We aimed to define the establishment rate of PDOs from patients with cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) and establish a protocol for the generation of PDOs from cryopreserved tissue.
METHODS: We established a biobank of PDOs from tumour tissues (N=26). A protocol for organoid establishment from cryopreserved tissue was optimised in mice, confirmed in human PDO, and validated across institutions.
RESULTS: While we started from a wide enrolment of different subtypes, including Pancreatic cancer (N=7), CCA (N=11), duodenal (N=2) and Ampullary Cancer (N=6), we refined the protocol towards biliary phenotype, with reduced efficiency rate in intestinal phenotype cancers. In total, 15 PDOs were established (58%); in the CCA cohort the efficiency rate of 75% (8 out of 11). Confirmation of organoid tumour origin was achieved through pathology review within a clinically-relevant time frame [median: 1.6 months (0.43-4.83 months)]. There was no numerical enrichment of successful PDO establishment for CCAs with poor prognostic factors such as perineural invasion, vascular invasion, nodal status and resection margins (p>0.05). Data from drug screening was ready within an average of 3 months from tissue collection (range:1.4-3.4 months). PDO from cryopreserved tissue was successful in 67% of cases and maintained the morphology, secretory functions, kinetic and dynamic growth patterns, transcriptomics, and drug sensitivity compared to organoids established from fresh tissues.
CONCLUSIONS: Cryopreserved tissue can facilitate the centralisation of PDO establishment and thus, the integration of biliary PDOs in multicentric trials.

title: MUC16 drives macrophage-mediated immunosuppression in pancreatic cancer.
abstract: Mucin-16 (MUC16) is overexpressed in >60% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cases and correlates with poor outcomes, yet its role in regulating tumor-immune interactions remains incompletely defined. Using KPC and KPC-MUC16 knockout (KPC-MUC16KO) genetically engineered and orthotopic mouse models, we show that loss of MUC16 markedly reduces tumor burden and reprograms the tumor microenvironment (TME) toward a less immunosuppressive state. MUC16 deficiency significantly decreased CD206+ and Ym1/2+ M2-like macrophages, increased the M1/M2 ratio, and improved survival. Cytokine profiling identified CCL2 and Serpin-E1 as MUC16- dependent secreted factors that promote macrophage recruitment and polarization; neutralization of these cytokines reduced macrophage migration in vitro. Bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDM) exposed to MUC16-expressing tumor cells or conditioned media adopted a CD206+Arg1+ M2-like phenotype, whereas MUC16KO tumor signals favored inflammatory CD86+iNOS+ M1-like polarization. Macrophage depletion using clodronate liposomes significantly impaired tumor growth in MUC16-competent tumors but had minimal effect in KPC-MUC16KO tumors, indicating dependence on macrophage-mediated immunosuppression in the former group. Spatial transcriptomics revealed a globally distinct TME in MUC16KO tumors, including enhanced antigen-presentation programs, increased complement activation, and fibroblast states skewed toward pro-inflammatory signaling. These findings establish MUC16 as a key orchestrator of macrophage-driven immunosuppression in PDAC and support therapeutic strategies combining MUC16-targeted interventions with TME-reprogramming approaches.

title: MF1, a novel robustic acid derivative, exerts antitumor effects in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) extensive genomic heterogeneity and immunosuppressive tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) are major factors contributing to treatment resistance. This study aims to elucidate the molecular mechanisms by which Robustic Acid 4-O-amino substituted synthetic derivatives (MF1), a novel robustic acid derivative, derived from structural modifications of natural products from Dalbergia benthamii Prain, targets carcinogenic signaling and synergistically regulates the crosstalk between autophagy and ferroptosis to induce programmed cell death in HCC. In vitro functional assays confirmed that MF1 exhibits significant antitumor activity. Mechanistically, MF1 significantly upregulates cellular oxidative stress levels, inducing characteristic changes in mitochondrial ultrastructure and apoptosis; simultaneously, by promoting intracellular Fe²⁺ accumulation and downregulating the expression of key ferroptosis regulators GPX4 and SLC7A11, it potently activates the ferroptosis process. Concurrently, MF1 continuously activates the cytotoxic autophagy pathway by regulating the LC3 I/II conversion ratio and upregulating the expression of core autophagy proteins ATG5 and Beclin-1. Network pharmacology identified 7 core targets of MF1 that are common to both ferroptosis and autophagy regulation. qPCR validation showed that MF1 significantly downregulated the mRNA expression of these 7 core oncogenes in HepG2 cells. Molecular docking confirmed strong binding affinities between MF1 and five core targets, 100 ns all-atom molecular dynamics simulations further validated the conformational stability of all five top-ranked MF1-protein complexes, with the higher binding stability for AKT1, SRC and MTOR. In summary, this study clarifies MF1 induces apoptosis and ferroptosis in HepG2 cells, suggesting its potential as a new therapeutic option for HCC.
